The eleven ratings for Vodafone

Vodafone Group (VOD-GB): a better business whose per-share story the market has over-credited

Date: 28 October 2026. Price: 118.25p (26 October; 52-week range 85.2p to 132.1p). Market capitalisation: about EUR 33bn. Next event: H1 FY27 results, 10 November 2026.

Fiscal years end 31 March (FY27 is the year to March 2027), and money is in euros unless stated. "Profit" means adjusted EBITDAaL (EBITDA after leases), the measure the company guides. The full conventions for profit, earnings per share, "our forecasts" and consensus are in the end notes.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in brief. Vodafone has finished the largest portfolio reset in European telecoms and has moved from surgery to harvest. Five forces now carry the business: a closed and wholly owned UK merger with GBP 1.0bn of synergies on a dated schedule; a consolidated African business growing 8 to 10 percent a year in local currency; a EUR 1.0bn net European cost programme; a balance sheet held at 2.2x to 2.4x net debt to EBITDAaL; and, from mid-2027, the largest shareholder in the sector with a record of forcing out costs (Xavier Niel's Vega, at 19.9 percent). On our forecasts, EBITDAaL grows from EUR 11.4bn in FY26 to EUR 15.0bn in FY31, and adjusted free cash flow grows from EUR 2.6bn to EUR 3.6bn.

The flaw in the case sits between EBITDAaL and the shareholder. Three narrowings dilute Vodafone's operating growth before it reaches earnings per share. First, Vodafone owns all of its shrinking German profit pool but only about a third of its fastest-growing one (Safaricom). Second, the FY26 earnings base was flattered by EUR 1.4bn of investment income on disposal cash, and that cash is now spent. Third, from FY28 about two-thirds of per-share growth comes from a EUR 2bn-a-year buyback that is half funded by debt.

The ten things that matter.

  1. Vodafone's operating forecasts are unusually predictable, but its EPS forecasts are not. We expect FY27 EBITDAaL to land inside the EUR 13.0bn to 13.3bn guidance range with about 85 percent confidence (our forecast is EUR 13.17bn). Four lines that the company does not guide (depreciation, financing, tax and minorities) absorb about 70 percent of EBITDAaL growth to FY31. Milestones for the case should therefore be set in EBITDAaL and cash, not in EPS.
  2. Safaricom adds about 10 percent to group EBITDAaL and close to nothing to EPS. Vodafone's economic share of Safaricom is only about 36 percent, Vodafone bought its additional stake with Kenyan-shilling debt costing 10 to 12 percent, and Safaricom's profit was already in Vodafone's earnings as associate income. For these three reasons, FY27 EPS is flat on FY26, and the full-year effect of the Safaricom consolidation in FY28 adds little more.
  3. The +21.5 percent step in consensus FY28 EPS is the market's main error. The consensus step needs the share of pre-tax profit lost to tax and minorities to fall while minority-heavy Africa grows fastest, and it carries forward FY26's EUR 819m net financing cost (we forecast EUR 1,550m for FY28). We expect consensus FY28 EPS to fall by 5 to 12 percent over 18 months, in two steps: when the H1 profit components are published in November 2026, and when FY28 guidance is given in May 2027.
  4. Germany is the structural negative in the case, and the market already discusses it fully. Vodafone Germany loses about 95,000 broadband lines a quarter to fibre; the court-ordered reversal of its EUR 5 price rise costs about EUR 60m a year plus EUR 100m to 200m of refunds; the boost from 1&1 wholesale income laps from Q2 FY27; and Vodafone's own plans assume that EUR 400m of 1&1 roaming revenue, earned at a 70 percent margin, will leave. We forecast German EBITDAaL to fall from EUR 4.15bn in FY26 to EUR 3.65bn in FY31.
  5. The UK is the cleanest chain of reasoning in the case. Management has raised the UK merger synergies to GBP 0.8bn by FY30 and GBP 1.0bn by FY32, is ahead of plan on organisation and retail savings, and precedent (MasOrange, Swisscom, E-Plus) favours delivery. We forecast UK EBITDAaL to rise from EUR 1.95bn in FY27, the year of merger dis-synergies, to EUR 2.65bn in FY31, and UK operating free cash flow to triple to over GBP 1.5bn by FY32. The two untested steps are the IT migration (due by end-2028) and the unwinding of the MBNL network-sharing joint venture (2030).
  6. Vodafone's capital loop amplifies results in both directions. At constant leverage of 2.3x to 2.4x, EBITDAaL growth creates about EUR 1bn a year of new debt capacity. That debt capacity, plus EUR 0.75bn to 1.2bn of organic cash after dividends, funds the EUR 2bn annual buyback, which retires 6 percent of the share count a year and adds about 4 percent a year to EPS after interest. If EBITDAaL stalls (because of Germany, 1&1 or currency), the buyback shrinks by more than the EBITDAaL shortfall.
  7. The upside catalysts are real and dated, but they are 6 to 18 months away. They are: FY28 guidance and the buyback decision in May 2027 (we see a 70 percent probability of a EUR 1.5bn to 2bn buyback); Vega's board representation after UK national-security clearance (summer 2027 at the earliest), with a possible doubling of the cost target (Morgan Stanley's scenario: +7 percent on FY30 EBITDAaL and +26 percent on free cash flow, in no broker's forecasts); UK pricing freedom when the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) tariff caps lapse in May 2028; and the Vantage Towers lease window in November 2028.
  8. The next six months carry the negative skew. The H1 results on 10 November 2026 will show the cost of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) price-rise ruling, the lap of German wholesale income, and the first post-Safaricom figures for minorities and financing. The FY27 guidance wording will most likely soften from "upper end" to "upper half". One-month revisions have already turned negative: consensus EPS is down 5 percent, and the share of Buy ratings has fallen to 33 percent.
  9. The guideline fair multiple of 15.99x is the least reliable element of the case. The 15.99x guideline is the 90th percentile of a ten-year history that includes 2016 to 2019, when Vodafone traded at 15x to 24x on depressed earnings and a EUR 50bn debt pile. My fair multiple is about 12x two-year-forward earnings (ten-year median 11.0x; five-year 75th percentile 10.2x; 13.4x "defendable" if Vega delivers). At 12x, the 18-month total return is about +15 to +20 percent, not the model's +56 percent.
  10. The stock sits on a plateau late in its thesis-broadening phase, not in a reinforcing phase. The dashboard's rule reads twelve-month momentum and therefore classifies the stock as Reinforcing. The last three months (price -4 percent, negative revisions, a beta of 1.5 to a de-rating sector) show that the broadening has stalled while the stock waits for the May 2027 catalysts.

Implication for Richard. Vodafone is a good business-change story whose per-share arithmetic the market has over-credited. From today's price, the fundamental outcomes are not unusually skewed to the positive: the probable developments of the next six months are either already in the price or negative to expectations, and the developments that could tilt the skew positive (the buyback, Vega, UK pricing) are dated after them. The setup that would make Vodafone unusually attractive is a reset, and that reset is a plausible state of the world in February to April 2027.

About 100pshare price: about 9x our FY28 EPS, the five-year median multiple

The five judgements that move the shares most (the arithmetic is in the section after #12): (1) the pace of German decline and the fate of the 1&1 wholesale contract; (2) the below-the-line reset (financing, minorities and tax) against consensus; (3) the size and funding of the FY28 buyback; (4) emerging-market currencies; and (5) a Vega-driven second cost programme. A sixth factor, the multiple, is worth more than any of the five: each turn of two-year-forward P/E is worth about 11p a share, or 9.5 percent of the share price.

Scorecard

#1Operating environment: tailwinds, and the absence of headwinds

Bottom lineThe operating environment sets the boundaries of the Vodafone case rather than driving it. The tailwinds are structural and already paid for by a share price up 33 percent in twelve months; the headwinds are narrower and sharper, and they are concentrated in Germany, the market that sets the group's value.

Evidence. Over the next twelve months the external picture is close to balanced and tilted slightly negative.

Tailwinds (structural, visible, priced)Headwinds (narrow, sharp, concentrated in Germany)
Regulation now permits in-market consolidation. The CMA cleared the merger with Three on behavioural remedies; the EU's final merger guidelines are due around 1 November 2026; German spectrum licences run to 2030, and UK spectrum is perpetual.Fibre is overbuilding Vodafone's German cable network. Deutsche Telekom passes 2.5 million homes a year with fibre, and alternative networks have passed 14.5 million homes.
German pricing has turned to value over volume. Deutsche Telekom raised back-book prices by EUR 2 to 3 in April 2026 with "manageable" churn, and 1&1 is withdrawing tariffs below EUR 7.The ECJ ruling of 10 September 2026 removed discretionary mid-contract price rises, in a case brought against Vodafone Germany specifically.
Africa grows on regulator-permitted price rises and on M-Pesa. Egypt's local-currency service revenue rose 32.9 percent in Q1 FY27; M-Pesa has 103 million users and processed USD 525bn.The UK is in a price fight. Virgin Media O2 has cut gigabit broadband to GBP 26.99 and giffgaff unlimited to GBP 14, fintech virtual operators run on Vodafone's own network, and CMA tariff caps apply until May 2028.
Satellite direct-to-device services are being disproved as a near-term European threat, and Vodafone participates in the technology through AST SpaceMobile.Vodafone has the largest emerging-market currency exposure among European telecoms: the rand, Egyptian pound and Turkish lira make up about 29 percent of revenue.
The market regime penalises leveraged yield stocks: the US ten-year yield is near 5.1 percent, markets are risk-off, and momentum investors are underweight.

Inference. Germany provides about 40 percent of underlying operating profit, so the headwinds hit the one market that sets the group's value. Three consequences follow for the forecasts. European revenue will be flat to slightly down. African revenue will grow in local currency and lose part of that growth in translation to euros. Every point of margin gain must therefore come from Vodafone's own actions.

So what. Do not pay for an environmental recovery. Our forecasts already assume no real (above-inflation) European price increases before May 2028, German broadband losses of about 380,000 in FY27 easing to about 250,000 a year, and a currency-translation drag of 1 to 1.5 points a year on group revenue.

Counter-case. Two developments could make the environment better than we assume. German value-over-volume pricing could hold up better, which is our bull case (German EBITDAaL falling 1 percent a year rather than 2.5 percent). The UK price fight could end sooner if Virgin Media O2's GBP 22bn of debt forces it to stop discounting.

What would change my view.

Upward

  • German broadband losses below 60,000 a quarter for two consecutive quarters.

Downward

  • A combination of Telefónica and 1&1 (about EUR 0.3bn of Vodafone's EBITDAaL at risk).
  • A Middle East escalation that weakens the Egyptian pound.

Market versus my view. I agree with the market on the facts of the environment and differ only in weighting. The sell-side articulates all of the factors above, and the German negatives are the most discussed dynamic in the case.

The market's frame

"A turnaround, with Germany as the problem."

My frame

"Germany is the largest profit pool, and the market structure there is consolidating against Vodafone." That is the frame investors applied to Liberty Global and Virgin Media O2, and the market has not yet applied it to Vodafone.

Score: 42. A supportive structure on paper (three-player markets, permissive regulators, African price floors) undermined by a fibre overbuild and a court ruling in the market that matters most.

#2Internally driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Bottom lineVodafone's internal change forces have been the strength of the case since 2023. The question is no longer whether those forces are strong but whether their next increments are new to estimates: the second wave is already in consensus, and only the third wave, driven by Vega, can lift estimates above it, from 2027.

Evidence. Vodafone's corporate change has come in three waves, set out below. Two details matter for the forecasts. The EUR 1.0bn net European cost programme already contains the UK operating-cost synergies, so adding the two together double-counts several hundred million euros. And at Tele2, Vega's precedent, the EBITDAaL gains faded from +11.4 percent in 2025 to about +3 percent by Q3 2026.

Problems. Four problems sit alongside the change programme.

  • No internal force addresses the German consumer franchise. Vodafone's fibre response is capital-light: the OXG fibre joint venture builds about 100,000 homes a quarter (and the swap of OXG partner forfeits up to EUR 1.1bn of deferred payments), Vodafone buys wholesale access to alternative fibre networks, and it upgrades its cable network (DOCSIS). That approach preserves cash and cedes market position.
  • Delivery has slipped once. H2 FY26 EBITDAaL missed consensus by about 2 percent, and management blamed Germany and headquarters costs.
  • Leadership is thin below the top. The chief executive is a 32-year insider with no designated successor, executive turnover during the integration is high, and experts describe the front line as fatigued.
  • Vega's timing is in regulators' hands. The UK national-security review may delay Vega's board seats to summer 2027, and banks hold part of Vega's stake pending approval.

So what. Three modelling rules follow, and our forecasts apply all three.

  1. Model margin expansion of 0.3 to 0.7 points a year from cost savings and synergies.
  2. Credit only about 65 percent of the net cost target to reported EBITDAaL. Proximus converted 38 percent of its gross savings into profit, Telia expects 70 percent, and Morgan Stanley says that less than half of Vodafone's own historical gross savings reached profit.
  3. Carry the Vega programme as an explicit upside scenario from FY29, not in the base case.

Counter-case. Management's first-wave record (disposals at good prices, 11,000 roles removed, guidance met three years running) argues that it will deliver the second wave on time, and that an owner-driven third wave could be larger and earlier than I allow.

What would change my view.

Upward

  • A named, dated second cost target.
  • UK operating-cost synergies above GBP 150m in year one.

Two-sided

  • A move by Vega to change management.

Downward

  • German broadband losses accelerating after customers receive the court-ordered price-reversal letters.

Market versus my view. The market sees the same three waves. I differ on two points. First, the market reads the resumed buyback as earnings growth, whereas I read it as the capital loop, which is half debt-funded and reversible. Second, our own first round of work treated the UK synergies and the EUR 1.0bn European target as additive; the same error is easy to make, which suggests that some sell-side models may also overstate the savings.

Score: 68. Among the strongest and best-executed corporate change programmes in European telecoms, with a credible third act, held back by the one market it does not fix.

#3Value chain, business model, financial profile and management

Bottom lineVodafone is a medium-quality business with above-average management, not a high-quality compounder. It is the advantaged player where profits are small and the disadvantaged player where profits are largest. That profile supports trusting the guided lines and the synergy timetables, and argues against paying a growth multiple.

Industry structure and position. Vodafone's industries are concentrated and still consolidating: there are three network owners each in Germany and the UK, and Vodacom and MTN hold about 75 percent of South Africa. Market shares are stable in mobile and in Africa, and unstable in German fixed broadband, where customers move to the fibre owner.

Vodafone's German wholesale income depends on a single customer. 1&1 pays about EUR 400m a year, with a contractual floor of EUR 50m a year, and 1&1's own network coverage is 34 percent, heading to 50 percent by 2030. Precedent is clear, and Vodafone carries both sides of it: closed mergers and owner-forced cost cuts have outperformed, while cable networks overbuilt by fibre (Liberty Global: -31 percent over twelve months) and dependence on a single wholesale customer have underperformed.

Competitive advantage. Vodafone's moats are widening where profits are small and narrowing where profits are large. The advantages are real in scale (EUR 25bn of central procurement), licences (perpetual in the UK; to 2030 in Germany), enterprise switching costs, UK spectrum and African network effects. They are absent in European consumer markets, where customer loyalty is low and Vodafone's network quality does not lead.

Financial profile. Vodafone's financial profile is below the sector average on returns, margins and earnings quality, and comfortable on credit.

Weaknesses for equity holdersStrengths
The UK business targets a ROCE above its cost of capital only by FY32.Cash tax has been genuinely low for decades and stays low (a EUR 15.2bn Luxembourg deferred tax asset).
No relief on capital intensity: BT and Orange harvest falling fibre capital spending, while Vodafone rents its German fibre, so peer comparisons should add the rent back.The credit is comfortable: BBB at all three rating agencies, more than 95 percent of debt at fixed rates, and a 13-year average maturity.
The widest gap between adjusted and reported earnings in the peer group: FY26 reported net income was EUR -289m against adjusted EUR 2,576m, after excluding restructuring, amortisation of acquired intangibles, hyperinflation and deferred-tax write-downs.
Minority leakage is rising with Safaricom, and the German trade-tax losses run out in four to five years.
Debt is material for equity: including leases, equity is only about 60 percent of enterprise value.

Management. Vodafone's management is above the peer median and well above Vodafone's own history. Judged by her actions, chief executive Margherita Della Valle is a strong operator and capital allocator: she executed the portfolio reset at good prices, has met guidance three years running, and bought the UK minority cheaply.

  • Alignment: her own shareholding stands at 91 percent of a requirement of 500 percent of salary, the highest in the peer group.
  • Ambition: deliberately modest, centred on cash, simplicity and returns, with no group revenue or EPS targets.
  • Communication: clear on the group and selective on Germany, where growth is presented without separating out the wholesale prop.
  • Culture: that of a restructured incumbent, aligned at the top and strained at the front line.
  • Incentives: the 2027 plan drops relative total shareholder return in favour of a 90 percent weighting on free cash flow, which pays management for cash even if the share price falls.

So what. Trust the guided lines and the synergy timetables, but do not pay a growth multiple. In our forecasts, segment margins rise in the UK and Africa and fall in Germany, and European prices rise no faster than inflation.

Counter-case. On a sum-of-the-parts view, the UK and Africa carry more quality than the group averages show. The UK is about 26 percent of Morgan Stanley's valuation, and Vodafone's African fintech business is twice the size of Airtel Money, which is listing at a valuation of USD 7bn to 9bn.

What would change my view. Upward: German network quality moving off last place in independent tests; a credible plan for Vodafone to own fibre in Germany; group ROCE rising through 7 percent.

Market versus my view. The market and I agree on the industry structure. I weight the German cable-overbuild precedent more heavily and the African fintech optionality less, because Vodafone's shareholders receive only 36 to 65 cents of each euro of African profit.

Score: 45. A concentrated, consolidating industry and a good management team attached to a below-average financial profile and a narrowing moat in the largest profit pool.

#4Conservative guidance, expectations management and the record of delivery

Bottom lineManagement is an "honest tracker": it sets ranges it can meet, steers to the top and raises once the evidence is in hand. Consensus has already moved to the top of the FY27 EBITDAaL range, so no cushion is left on profit, a modest one remains on cash, and the company guides nothing below EBITDAaL, which is where the market's expectations are wrong.

Evidence: the guidance. The company raised its FY27 guidance at Q1 and has given mid-term targets for cash.

Evidence: the record. Management's record looks different against its own guidance than against consensus. Against its own guidance, management has delivered since FY24, after a poor five years before. Against consensus, EBITDAaL has missed by 1 to 2 percent in most years, with the misses clustered in Germany, while cash has beaten; the FY26 cash beat of 3 percent came partly from deferred restructuring spending, which reverses in FY27.

Management's informal commentary runs ahead of its guidance on Germany ("stabilisation") and on the UK ("highly confident"). Two negatives that arrived after the FY27 raise, the ECJ ruling and the change of OXG partner, have not yet been absorbed publicly.

Inference. Vodafone is not a sandbagger like Deutsche Telekom or Orange, which raise guidance repeatedly within the year. On profit, consensus EBITDAaL (EUR 13,275m) has already moved to the top of the FY27 range. On cash, a modest cushion remains: the top of the guided range is about 9 percent above the company-compiled consensus of mid-September.

So what. Anchor FY27 EBITDAaL in the upper half of guidance less a German adjustment: our EUR 13.17bn is EUR 130m below the top of the range and EUR 80m below Morgan Stanley's post-ruling figure. Anchor FY27 cash in the upper half of its range (our EUR 2.85bn).

For the FY27 results in May 2027, we expect three announcements: FY28 EBITDAaL guidance of roughly EUR 13.7bn to 14.1bn (around our EUR 13.9bn and below consensus at EUR 14.1bn); FY28 adjusted free cash flow guidance of EUR 3.0bn to 3.3bn; and a buyback of EUR 1.5bn to 2bn (70 percent probability).

Counter-case. A fourth consecutive cash beat is more likely than not. The cash record is three years of beats; Egypt and Turkey are running ahead of plan; the rand is stronger than the ZAR 19.60 rate assumed in guidance (a EUR 60m tailwind on Deutsche Bank's sizing); and energy costs are hedged for FY27.

What would change my view.

Downward

  • Guidance wording moving to "upper half" (a small negative, already in our numbers).
  • An explicit statement that restructuring cash will exceed EUR 0.7bn (negative: outside the adjusted free cash flow measure but inside net debt).

Headline only

  • A Kenyan Court of Appeal ruling that forces Vodafone to de-consolidate Safaricom would cut headline EBITDAaL by EUR 1.4bn at a stroke but EPS by only 1 to 2 percent. Investors should prepare for the headline.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Bottom lineCost is the lever that works for Vodafone, and price is the lever that does not. Operating and financial leverage are both high, but the revenue that is growing is shared with minorities while the revenue that is shrinking is wholly owned, so from FY28 per-share growth is a capital-structure story.

Pricing power. Vodafone has real pricing power only in Africa, where regulators permit inflation pass-through, and in the German front book, where average revenue per new broadband customer is up 30 percent, paid for with lost volume. Elsewhere, the price levers have gone: the court has removed the German back-book lever, Ofcom and the CMA cap UK prices until May 2028, and Portugal is in a price war with Digi. The sector rule that "pricing power is a clause written at signing" now governs Vodafone's two largest markets. Price adds 1.5 to 2 points a year to nominal group revenue, almost all of it in Africa and Turkey, where currency translation then takes it back, and it adds about nothing to margin.

Operating leverage. Vodafone's operating leverage is material and works in both directions, because its cost base is largely fixed.

  • In reverse, operating leverage has already cost Germany EUR 1.1bn. German EBITDAaL fell 21 percent in three years because the lost TV revenue carried 85 percent margins. The ECJ price reversal (near 100 percent margin) and the 1&1 roaming income (70 percent margin) are the next two tests.
  • Forward, operating leverage works in the UK and Africa. UK synergies fall on a fixed network being cut from 37,000 to 26,000 sites, and African data and M-Pesa revenue grow on an existing network.
  • Depreciation is the hidden fixed cost. Depreciation and amortisation of owned assets rises from EUR 7.8bn to EUR 8.35bn, so EBIT margin rises less than EBITDAaL margin.

Financial leverage. Vodafone holds leverage at 2.3x to 2.4x and uses the capacity rather than paying debt down. Because adjusted net income is only about 18 percent of EBITDAaL, 1 percent of EBITDAaL is about 4 percent of EPS. Interest costs are largely fixed (only EUR 9m of pre-tax profit per 100 basis points on the floating-rate debt), but refinancing is a growing drag: EUR 14.8bn of debt matures within two years of March 2026 at coupons 1 to 2.5 points above the bonds it replaces (a drag of 3 to 5 percent of EPS by FY29), and a further EUR 10bn matures in FY30 and FY31. At today's share price the buyback earns a 7.8 percent earnings yield against a 3 percent after-tax cost of debt, so the buyback adds about 4 percent a year to EPS, net of interest.

Cost scope. The scope to cut costs is large and specific. The current programme is EUR 1.0bn net (EUR 2.0bn gross) through FY30, with the UK's GBP 1.0bn of synergies inside that figure, and it leaves the EUR 10bn emerging-market cost base untouched. A Tele2-style programme could plausibly double the net saving over four to five years. Gross savings are not net savings, however: the target's definition excludes energy and exceptional wage costs, and German revenue erodes at high margin against the savings.

Feedback loops. Four feedback loops shape the forecasts, and their ownership is asymmetric, which is the key to the forecasts. The German cable loop is reinforcing, negative, slow and 100 percent owned. The German wholesale loop is balancing, with a cliff, because Vodafone plans for 1&1 to leave. The M-Pesa loop is reinforcing, positive and strong, but reaches Vodafone at about 36 cents in the euro. The capital loop reinforces in both directions (second figure below).

Inference. Revenue growth does produce outsized profit growth at Vodafone, but because the growing revenue is minority-shared and the shrinking revenue is wholly owned, group EBITDAaL growth overstates growth attributable to Vodafone's shareholders by about a point a year. Management has demonstrated that it can remove central costs, so cost is the lever to back.

Counter-case: the single largest upside in the case, and it is not in consensus. A doubled cost programme, reaching the accounts at even 50 percent conversion, would add about EUR 1bn of wholly owned European EBITDAaL by FY31, which is 25 to 30 percent of EPS.

What would change my view. Upward: evidence that German front-book prices can carry indexation clauses after the court ruling; a UK pricing move after May 2028; a cost target with a geographic split and a net definition that includes energy.

Market versus my view. The market knows the German loop and the Vega option. The market does not articulate two things: the ownership asymmetry (Safaricom has close to zero effect on EPS) and the debt funding of the buyback. No broker found in our narrative research states that the buyback relies on debt capacity created by EBITDAaL growth, or that the buyback shrinks if EBITDAaL stalls.

Score: 48. Strong cost-out scope and high operating and financial leverage, but no European pricing power and loops whose ownership runs the wrong way.

#6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and for better growth and margins than the past

Bottom lineVodafone's operating growth is real but low (about 3 percent a year organically), and very little of it reaches attributable net income. Double-digit EPS growth from FY29 exists on paper, but it is bought with debt-funded buybacks, and our EPS forecasts sit 10 to 11 percent below consensus for FY28 and FY29.

By segment. Germany is the only segment whose EBITDAaL falls between FY27 and FY31; Africa and the UK supply most of the increase.

Where the growth comes from, FY26 to FY31. EBITDAaL rises EUR 3.7bn, but attributable net income rises only EUR 0.3bn.

Safaricom supplies EUR 1.55bn of the EBITDAaL increase, 42 percent of the net change, yet that profit reaches Vodafone's shareholders at only about 36 cents in the euro. Three lines then absorb most of the remaining growth before net income. Depreciation rises by about EUR 1.1bn. Net financing costs rise by about EUR 0.9bn from a flattered FY26 base: the FY26 cost of EUR 819m was net of EUR 1,395m of investment income on disposal cash and on the Spanish preference shares, and that income is now spent. Minorities rise by about EUR 0.65bn, from EUR 194m. EPS still rises 45 percent, but about two-thirds of that increase comes from the falling share count and only one-third from the business.

Scope for double-digit growth. Only the per-share lines reach double digits, and they get there through the share count.

MeasureDouble-digit growth?Why
EPSYes: 11 to 12 percent a year from FY29almost entirely from buybacks
Adjusted free cash flow per shareYes: 10 to 14 percent a year from FY28cash growth plus a falling share count
EBITDAaLNo: about 3 percent organiccost savings and the UK, offset by Germany
RevenueNo: 2 to 3 percentno real price increases in Europe

Compared with the past four years (flat EBITDA, with EPS lifted by tax, depreciation and the share count), the coming four years are a clear break at the operating line and the same story per share.

Against consensus. Our forecasts are close to consensus on revenue and EBITDAaL and well below it on EPS. Our revenue is 1.6 percent below consensus each year, because we forecast lower revenue in Germany and Turkey. Our EBITDAaL is 0.8, 1.4 and 3.8 percent below consensus for FY27, FY28 and FY29, because we do not credit a 31.6 percent margin by FY29. Our EPS is in line with consensus for FY27, then 11 percent below for FY28 and 10 percent below for FY29. Three below-the-line lines explain the EPS gap:

Our cone of outcomes over 18 months. We expect FY27 EBITDAaL of EUR 13.0bn to 13.3bn (85 percent confidence) and FY28 EBITDAaL of EUR 13.4bn to 14.3bn. For FY28 EPS, our bear case is EUR 0.095, our base EUR 0.114 and our bull EUR 0.133. The risks are balanced around our base case and negative around consensus, because consensus sits at our bull case (see the cone chart in #7).

What would change the forecasts.

Upward

  • German broadband losses below 60,000 a quarter for two quarters.
  • A dated second cost target.
  • UK synergies ahead of plan.
  • A disclosed reconciliation showing that part of FY26's investment income recurs.

Downward

  • German service revenue falling more than 2 percent in a quarter.
  • A Telefónica-1&1 deal.
  • Leverage above 2.5x in March 2027.
  • FY28 guidance without a buyback.

Score: 40. Double-digit per-share growth exists on paper but is bought with debt-funded buybacks; operating growth is low single digits; the forecasts are modestly below consensus on profit and clearly below on EPS.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Bottom lineOver the next 6 to 12 months, the probable revisions are negative on FY28 EPS, the line the market quotes. The positive revisions (Vega's cost target, UK pricing freedom, the Vantage Towers window) are dated beyond that window, in months 12 to 36.

Evidence. Guidance leaves no cushion on FY27 EBITDAaL, because consensus sits at the top of the range; it leaves a modest cushion on cash and says nothing below EBITDAaL. Consensus FY28 EPS of EUR 0.130 requires three below-the-line lines (minorities, financing and tax) to behave better than the FY26 components say they will. Two events will test that requirement:

  • The H1 results on 10 November 2026 will show, for the first time, the minorities created by the Safaricom consolidation and the net financing line after the disposal cash has been spent.
  • The FY27 results in May 2027 will set FY28 guidance in the honest-tracker style, probably bracketing our EUR 13.9bn of EBITDAaL rather than consensus at EUR 14.1bn.

The market narrative covers Germany, 1&1, the UK and Vega in detail. It does not cover the effect of minority leakage on EPS, the debt funding of the buyback, or the steps in refinancing cost and German trade tax in FY30 and FY31.

Inference. We expect estimate revisions over the next 6 to 12 months to run in three different directions by line:

LineExpected revision, 6 to 12 months
FY28 and FY29 EPSDown 5 to 12 percent
FY28 and FY29 EBITDAaLFlat to down 1 to 4 percent
CashFlat to up

The narrative will shift from "self-help that has been paid for" to "what will the new owner force". Until Vega is seated on the board, that question is a hope, not a number.

So what. Within the next 6 to 12 months, the scope for upgrades is confined to three sources:

  1. a fourth consecutive cash beat;
  2. a currency tailwind, where each 10 percent strengthening of the rand and Egyptian pound adds about EUR 70m to 110m of EBITDAaL;
  3. the May 2027 buyback announcement, which upgrades the per-share line mechanically (EUR 2bn at EUR 1.40 a share retires 6 percent of the share count).

Counter-case. Two of the three Buy cases among brokers (Deutsche Bank at EUR 1.89 and Goldman Sachs at EUR 1.80) rest on the look-through value of the UK synergies and African growth, and a Vega announcement could arrive with the FY27 results if UK clearance comes early. The EPS cuts I expect are also largely definitional, and the market has already half-discounted them: the consensus rating is Hold, and the mean target price is at the share price.

What would change my view. Upward: a Vega-related announcement before May 2027; FY28 EBITDAaL guidance set above consensus; H1 components showing minorities below EUR 250m for the half.

Market versus my view: the largest difference between my view and consensus, and it is adverse. The market expects guidance to be met and the buyback to return, and so do I. The market expects FY28 EPS of EUR 0.130; I expect consensus FY28 EPS to be cut toward EUR 0.115 to 0.123, in two steps.

Score: 35. The probable revisions of the next six to twelve months are negative on the line the market quotes; the positive revisions are dated beyond the window.

#8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, technicals, and peers

Bottom lineVodafone has had the best twelve months in its sector, and its momentum has now paused on every measure: estimates, ratings and price. The stock re-rated on its own news against a de-rating sector, and with a beta of 1.5 it would fall half again as hard as its peers in a sector sell-off.

Evidence. Each of the six momentum measures shows strong twelve-month gains that have stalled.

MeasureReading
GuidanceOne raise (July 2026) and none since; two negatives (the ECJ ruling and the OXG partner change) not yet absorbed.
EstimatesFY27 EPS revisions +14 percent over twelve months, +10 percent over three months and -5 percent over one month; EBITDA -2 percent over one month. The dashboard's fixed grade for sell-side momentum is D.
Ratings and targetsBuy ratings are 33 percent of the total, down 4 points in a month and up 15 points over three months. The mean target price is EUR 1.45 against a share price of EUR 1.42. Brokers split three Buys, two Holds and three Sells (figure below).
NarrativeThe narrative turned positive in July (Vega's stake) and in October (the UK investor day, described as "calm, clear and confident"); the ECJ ruling and the Kenyan High Court case are the counterweights.
TechnicalsShare price +32.8 percent over twelve months (relative strength percentile 59) and -4.1 percent over three months; below the 50-day average (122.8p) and 3 percent above the 200-day average (114.5p, which has risen in each of the last twelve months); 10 percent below the October high. The dashboard's fixed technical grade is C.
PeersDeutsche Telekom trades at the 1st percentile of its own P/E history and Telefónica at the 9th; all five large peers have a technical grade of F. Vodafone's six-month beta to the sector is 1.50, the highest in 24 months, with 65 percent of its share price variance specific to Vodafone.

Inference. Vodafone's momentum came from its own news, not from the sector, and that independence now cuts both ways. A beta of 1.5 means that a sector sell-off (triggered by higher rates, French and Italian sovereign stress, or disappointing EU merger guidelines) would hit Vodafone half again as hard as the sector. Peers trade at trough multiples with falling estimates, so the sector offers Vodafone no momentum support.

So what. Momentum is neutral to negative for the next two results events, and could turn positive at the May 2027 results if the buyback is announced. Position sizing should respect two sources of volatility: the 1.5 beta, and Vega's partly bank-financed stake (a holder who bought at 112.5p can sell, hedge or agitate).

Counter-case. The technical damage is shallow. The 200-day average has risen for twelve months, the pullback from 132p has been orderly, and the stock has held above its level at the July guidance raise. Three-month revisions are still positive, and the one-month turn reflects one broker's reaction to the ECJ ruling.

What would change my view. Upward: a close above the 50-day average after an H1 report that keeps the "upper end" wording. Downward: a break below 110p that turns the 200-day average down.

Market versus my view. The dashboard's fixed grades (technical C, sell-side D) match my reading. I would add that a consensus target price equal to the share price is the clearest statement that the sell-side sees no upside on its own numbers.

Score: 40. Strong trailing momentum that has stalled on estimates, ratings and price, with high beta to a sector in a down-trend.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Bottom lineThe operating case is simple and trackable; the per-share case is a chain of four links, each hanging on an external event. The largest sudden risks to EPS are emerging-market currencies and a German consolidation, and a 1.5 beta amplifies the sector's sensitivity to interest rates.

Simplicity of the case. At the operating level the case is simple. Three drivers (the Safaricom consolidation, the UK merger and its synergies, and African organic growth) supply nine-tenths of EBITDAaL growth, and each is announced and mechanical. At the per-share level the case is complex. It runs through a chain of four links (minorities, financing, tax and the buyback), and each link depends on an external event: a Kenyan court, a German competitor, the bond market, or a board decision in May 2027.

Definitions add noise of their own. Across the twelve visible brokers, FY27 EPS forecasts run from EUR 0.080 to 0.150 and FY28 forecasts from EUR 0.097 to 0.170, on EBITDA forecasts that differ by only 3 percent. A reported "miss" against consensus EPS can therefore be a reclassification, and we expect at least one such episode in the next three results.

Fragilities and requirements. Our base case is more plausible than the bull case because it needs fewer things to go right.

The base case requires

  • Net drop-through of about a third of gross savings (Vodafone's 2022 to 2026 savings record coincided with flat EBITDAaL).
  • UK IT migration by end-2028 (Virgin Media O2 had captured 30 percent of its synergy target by the equivalent date).
  • A EUR 2bn buyback, half of it funded by debt.
  • Currencies no worse than the guidance rates.
  • Germany declining at about 2.5 percent a year, not 6 percent.

The base case does not require

  • Retention of German retail customers.
  • European pricing power.
  • A Vega cost programme.

Sudden, material risks, ranked. Currency and a German consolidation are the largest sudden risks to EPS; the Kenyan appeal would cut the headline far more than EPS.

Trackability. The operating case is easy to track; the EPS bridge is not. Quarterly data cover German KPIs, UK churn and customer additions, roles removed, 1&1's own site counts, Deutsche Telekom's fibre additions and Vodacom's updates. The EPS bridge is reported only half-yearly, is not guided, and has no split by subsidiary.

Sector and cyclicality precedents. Demand is barely cyclical (four-fifths of revenue is subscription), but the shares are highly sensitive to interest rates as a yield proxy, and the sector has a thirteen-year base rate of underperformance. Vodafone's own missed years were 2022 to 2023, when energy costs of EUR 760m faced a EUR 400m rise as hedges expired and the German TV law cost three times the initial estimate. Milder versions of both conditions are present again: energy hedges roll in FY27 and FY28, and the ECJ has removed high-margin revenue. History therefore says that the provision for these risks is more likely too small than too large.

Downside to a fair trough. On unchanged earnings, the five-year 25th-percentile multiple (8.28x) implies a share price 17 percent below today's (about 98p). With a 10 percent EPS cut, the same multiple implies 25 to 30 percent downside (83p to 89p), near the 52-week low of 85p. Bernstein's suspended 65p target and the option-implied floor of 88p (January 2026) bracket the tail.

Score: 45. A simple, trackable operating case attached to a noisy per-share line, a concentrated and partly external risk list, and an amplified sensitivity to the sector's rate regime.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Bottom lineVodafone sits on a plateau late in its thesis-broadening phase, between two legs. The second leg (the buyback, Vega, FY28 guidance) is six to nine months away, and the interval is filled with events of negative skew, so a pullback is more likely than a breakout before May 2027.

Evidence. The stock has passed through three phases in three years (figure below). Thesis broadening ran from January to October 2026 on Vega's stake, the Q1 beat and guidance raise, the Safaricom consolidation and the UK investor day; consensus FY28 EPS rose 17 percent in twelve months, and the multiple stood at 11.3x in February and 11.0x in July. Since October the evidence has turned: the price is down 4 percent over three months and 10 percent off its high, one-month revisions are negative, the share of Buy ratings is falling, the ECJ and Kenyan rulings and the OXG change have landed, and consensus has used up the guidance raise. The dashboard's rule, which reads twelve-month momentum, still classifies the stock as Reinforcing.

Inference. The stock is not in a reinforcing phase, because a reinforcing phase needs guidance, estimates and the price all rising together, and all three have stopped. Nor is the stock stalling in the structural sense: group fundamentals are not deteriorating, the drivers are intact, and the next catalysts are real and dated. The best description is a plateau between two legs.

So what. A plateau in a stock with a 1.5 beta to a de-rating sector is more likely to resolve down than up before May 2027, and a resolution down would provide the entry point the case needs. If the second leg arrives (a buyback announced, Vega seated on the board, a new cost target), the stock would move from broadening into a genuine reinforcing phase in FY28, and the fair multiple would rise with it.

Counter-case. Phase rules are deliberately mechanical, to avoid exactly this kind of judgement, and twelve-month revisions and the twelve-month price change are both strongly positive. A fourth cash beat in November and a clean H1 report would restart the broadening without a pullback.

What would change my view. Toward a reinforcing phase: FY28 EPS consensus holding above EUR 0.125 after the H1 components are published; a Vega announcement before May 2027. Toward a stall: German service revenue falling more than 2 percent in a quarter; the 200-day average turning down.

Market versus my view. The dashboard says Reinforcing, while the sell-side's Hold consensus and its target at the share price imply a plateau. I side with the sell-side's implicit view, for a stated reason: the increments the market can see over the next six months are not new.

Score: 50. A plateau in the late part of a thesis-broadening phase, with a credible second leg ahead but not yet in sight.

#11The fair multiple

Bottom lineMy fair multiple is about 12x two-year-forward earnings, with 13.4x as the upside case and 9x as the downside case. The guideline's 16x describes what the stock could reach at a peak, not what it is worth through the cycle.

The guideline. The Phases page assigns Vodafone to the Reinforcing phase and gives a guideline fair multiple of 15.99x two-year-forward earnings, the 90th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history. The ten-year bands are: 10th percentile 7.5x ("crash"); median 11.0x ("prudent"); 75th percentile 13.4x ("defendable"); 90th percentile 16.0x ("mania"). Today the stock trades at 10.7x consensus earnings and at 12.3x our lower EPS, so the guideline is 49 percent above the consensus-basis multiple.

Four reasons for about 12x rather than 16x.

  1. The ten-year range is distorted by 2016 to 2019. In those years the stock traded at 15x to 24x on earnings depressed by the Unitymedia-era balance sheet (net debt near EUR 50bn and leverage above 3x) and by heavy depreciation. Those multiples described a different company with different earnings, so they are not evidence of what the market will pay for today's Vodafone. On the five-year series the range is 7.0x to 12.2x, the median is 9.23x, and today's multiple sits at the 69th percentile.
  2. The stock's phase argues for the middle of its range, not the top. The stock is on a plateau late in thesis broadening, not in a reinforcing or peak-delivery phase. Richard's own rule places peak-delivery stocks high in their range and stocks with uncertain forecasts low. Vodafone's EPS forecasts are the least certain line in the case, and the market's EPS forecasts are too high. Both points argue for the band between the median and the 75th percentile, not for the 90th percentile.
  3. The market pays Vodafone a company-specific premium, but not a sector-high one. The dashboard's co-movement analysis shows that Vodafone's multiple is driven by company news, and that the market has paid a company-specific premium for cash gains in management's hands (the UK) and for the Vega option. It does not show that the market will pay a sector-high multiple for a group whose largest market is in structural decline and a third of whose profit is minority-shared and earned in emerging markets. The sector trades at trough multiples: Deutsche Telekom 9.1x (its 1st percentile), Telefónica 8.0x, BT 10.6x and Orange 11.3x. Only Telia (16.1x) and Tele2 (17.0x), Nordic operators after activist campaigns and with no emerging-market exposure, trade where the guideline puts Vodafone. At 16x, Vodafone would be the most expensive large incumbent in Europe.
  4. Activist-driven re-ratings are given back. Tele2 peaked at 13x EV/EBITDAaL in early 2026 and fell to 11.1x by October as further savings got harder; its share price rose 70 percent and then fell 17 percent. The premium is earned for two to three years and then returned, so a fair multiple should sit where the stock would trade through that cycle, not at its peak.

The arithmetic of my band. The band is applied to two-year-forward EPS at the 18-month column, a blend of FY29 and FY30 on our numbers of about EUR 0.13. At 11.0x the shares are worth EUR 1.43 (about 124p); at 12x, EUR 1.56 (about 136p); at 13.4x, EUR 1.74 (about 151p). At the five-year 25th percentile (8.3x) on a cut FY28 EPS of EUR 0.105, the shares are worth about 76p. Each turn of P/E is worth about 11p a share, 9.5 percent of today's price.

Where I agree with the guideline. If the second leg arrives in full (a dated Vega cost target, EUR 2bn buybacks and FY28 guidance above consensus), the stock would enter a true reinforcing phase, and the "defendable" 13.4x would be the right anchor for FY28. The guideline's 16x would then be the mania band that a Tele2-style run could touch and give back.

What would change my view.

Toward 13.4x or above

  • Vega seated on the board with a cost target.
  • UK pricing freedom used from May 2028.
  • The Airtel Money listing establishing a fintech multiple that the market applies to Vodacom.

Toward 9x

  • 1&1 leaving Vodafone's network.
  • A currency shock that stops the buyback.
  • FY28 guidance without a buyback.

Score: 40. The stock already trades in the upper third of its relevant range while its EPS forecasts are the least reliable part of the case; the guideline multiple is a peak, not a fair value.

#12Total shareholder return (Dupont split)

Bottom lineAlmost all of the model's +56 percent 18-month return comes from re-rating the shares to the guideline 16x. At my fair 12x, the probability-weighted 18-month return is about +13 percent (roughly 9 percent a year), with a wide cone, and it is driven by buybacks and the dividend rather than operating growth.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (15.99x). From 119p on 27 October 2026, the model returns +55.7 percent to the 18-month column (30 September 2027; a value of 185p; +61.5 percent annualised) and +89.6 percent to the three-year column (31 March 2029; a value of 225p; +30.2 percent annualised). The figure shows the template's split of each return into dividends, the multiple and earnings.

What drives the model's return, in plain terms. Almost all of the model's return is the re-rating. On the consensus basis the multiple rises from 10.7x to 16.0x (+49 percent); on the model's own EPS it rises from 12.3x to 16.0x (+30 percent). Our EPS is flat in FY27, +6 percent in FY28 and +11 percent in FY29, so the roll-forward of two-year-forward EPS from about EUR 0.11 today to about EUR 0.13 by September 2027 is worth about +15 to +20 percent. The dividend adds about 3.5 percent a year (4.1p on 118p). Everything above about +20 percent over 18 months is therefore the multiple. The template attributes more of the return to "earnings" and less to "the multiple" because it measures the multiple from the model's 12.3x starting point and rolls forward on its own convention; the economic reading is the one given here.

Three points to hold in mind when reading the model's figure.

  1. The model capitalises our EPS, which is 10 percent below consensus (FY29 EUR 0.126; FY30 EUR 0.141). If the market capitalised consensus EPS at the same multiple, the return would be higher still; if it capitalised our bear case (FY29 EUR 0.107), the return would be about 15 points lower.
  2. The exit multiple is the whole question. At my 12x, the 18-month total return is about +15 to +20 percent (136p plus about 6p of dividends). At 13.4x it is about +33 percent; at 11.0x about +10 percent; at the five-year median (9.2x) on unchanged EPS about -2 percent; and at the trough (8.3x on a cut EPS) about -30 percent.
  3. The earnings leg is itself a capital-structure leg. About 6 points of the +11 percent EPS growth in FY29 come from the buyback. A buyback halved to EUR 1bn removes about 3 points a year, and a buyback executed at EUR 1.70 a share instead of EUR 1.40 (after a re-rating) buys 15 percent fewer shares.

The probability-weighted picture over 18 months, my view. Weighting a bear case (25 percent), a base case (55 percent) and a bull case (20 percent) gives an expected return of about +13 percent, roughly 9 percent annualised.

Over three years, the return is attractive but not exceptional. If the second leg arrives, a 6 percent annual reduction in the share count, 3 percent organic EBITDAaL growth and a 4 percent dividend yield compound to a low-teens annual return at a constant 12x multiple. That return is attractive for a stock of this quality, but it is not the +30 percent a year that the guideline implies.

Market versus my view. The sell-side's mean target of EUR 1.45 (about 126p) offers 6 percent upside plus the dividend, close to my 11x case. Only Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs are near the model's 18-month value. I sit between the sell-side and the model, nearer the sell-side.

Score: 45. A respectable return at a fair multiple, driven by buybacks and the dividend rather than operating growth; the model's +56 percent rests on a multiple the stock's relevant history does not support.

±The key judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic

Bottom lineThe below-the-line reset is the largest gap to the market, Germany and 1&1 the largest wholly owned swing, currencies the largest sudden risk, and a Vega cost programme the largest upside. The multiple outweighs all five.

The base and the working rule. The sensitivities below use our FY28 base (EBITDAaL EUR 13,907m, attributable net income EUR 2,554m, average shares 22,428m, EPS EUR 0.114) and our FY29 base (EBITDAaL EUR 14,287m, shares 21,080m, EPS EUR 0.126). The working rule: EUR 100m of wholly owned EBITDAaL, taxed at 27 percent, becomes EUR 73m of net income, about 0.33 eurocents of FY28 EPS (2.9 percent). Only 55 to 65 percent of a change in African EBITDAaL reaches Vodafone's shareholders, and only about 36 percent of a change in Safaricom's.

Judgement 1: the pace of German decline and the fate of 1&1 (the largest wholly owned swing).

  • Base: German EBITDAaL of EUR 3.98bn (FY27), EUR 3.88bn (FY28) and EUR 3.78bn (FY29), with 1&1 income fading by EUR 0.1bn a year from FY29.
  • If Germany falls 6 percent a year instead of 2.5 percent: FY28 EBITDAaL is EUR 0.14bn lower, net income EUR 0.10bn lower and EPS 0.45 cents lower (-4 percent); FY29 EBITDAaL is EUR 0.26bn lower and EPS 0.9 cents lower (-7 percent).
  • If 1&1 leaves in full by FY29 (through a Telefónica purchase or faster self-supply): EBITDAaL is EUR 0.3bn lower (net of the EUR 0.1bn fade already modelled) and EPS 1.0 cent lower (-8 percent). The EUR 0.1bn to 0.2bn of capital spending saved helps cash, not EPS.
  • Both together: FY29 EPS of about EUR 0.107 (-15 percent). The bull case (Germany falling 1 percent a year): FY29 EPS 0.4 cents higher (+3 percent).
  • Watch: German broadband and contract net additions each quarter; 1&1's active site count and the BNetzA spectrum-sharing decision (Q4 2026); Telefónica's talks with 1&1.

Judgement 2: the below-the-line reset against consensus (the largest gap to the market).

  • The gap: consensus FY28 net income is EUR 3,144m against our EUR 2,554m, a gap of EUR 590m, 2.6 cents of EPS and 23 percent of our EPS.
  • Financing: we carry EUR 1,550m against FY26's EUR 819m. If half of FY26's investment income recurs (financing of EUR 1,250m), net income rises EUR 220m and EPS 1.0 cent (+9 percent). If refinancing costs run 100 basis points worse on EUR 15bn, net income falls EUR 110m and EPS 0.5 cents (-4 percent).
  • Minorities: we carry EUR 700m; consensus implies EUR 400m to 560m. Each EUR 100m is worth 0.45 cents (4 percent), so minorities of EUR 450m would add 1.1 cents to EPS.
  • Tax: a 27 percent rate rather than 25 percent, on pre-tax profit of EUR 3.5bn, is EUR 70m, or 0.3 cents.
  • Where consensus lands: all three lines in consensus's favour give about EUR 0.138, which is consensus. Only one in its favour gives EUR 0.124 to 0.125, the likely landing point of consensus over 18 months.
  • Watch: the H1 FY27 components on 10 November 2026, namely adjusted net financing cost and adjusted non-controlling interests for the half.

Judgement 3: the size and funding of the buyback (the engine of per-share growth).

  • Base: EUR 2bn a year from FY28 at EUR 1.40 a share buys about 1.43bn shares, 6.2 percent of the count. The effect is half a year in FY28 (+3 percent to EPS) and a full year in FY29 (+6 percent), compounding to a 23 percent lower share count by FY31 (+31 percent to EPS).
  • Funding: organic cash after dividends supplies about EUR 0.75bn (FY28) and EUR 1.2bn (FY29). The balance, EUR 1.25bn and EUR 0.8bn, comes from debt capacity at constant leverage, and that capacity (about EUR 1bn a year) exists only while EBITDAaL grows about 3 percent a year.
  • If the buyback is EUR 1bn: FY28 EPS is 1.5 percent lower (-0.2 cents), FY29 4.5 percent lower (-0.6 cents) and FY31 9 percent lower (-1.4 cents). If there is no buyback in May 2027: FY29 EPS is about EUR 0.119 (-6 percent), and the capital loop runs in reverse.
  • If the shares re-rate to EUR 1.70 before the programme: EUR 2bn buys 1.18bn shares (5.1 percent), and FY29 EPS is about 1 percent lower than modelled.
  • Watch: leverage at March 2027 (above 2.5x puts the buyback at risk); the FY27 results statement in May 2027.

Judgement 4: emerging-market currencies (the largest sudden risk).

  • The annual report's sensitivities: a 10 percent move in the Egyptian pound changes pre-tax profit by EUR 68m, in the rand by EUR 41m and in the lira by EUR 40m. After tax and minorities, the three together are worth about EUR 65m of attributable profit, 0.3 cents (2.5 to 3 percent of FY28 EPS).
  • A 20 percent fall in the basket: EBITDAaL falls EUR 0.67bn (-5 percent, enough to cut FY27 guidance) and EPS 0.6 cents (-5 to 6 percent). Leverage rises to about 2.5x (EUR 31.5bn over EUR 12.5bn), which halves the buyback (Judgement 3). The combined FY29 effect is about -1.2 cents (-10 percent).
  • A 10 percent strengthening (the rand is already stronger than the ZAR 19.60 guidance rate): EBITDAaL rises EUR 70m to 110m in a year, enough to trigger a guidance raise.
  • Watch: oil and the Middle East for the Egyptian pound; the rand against ZAR 19.60.

Judgement 5: a Vega-driven second cost programme (the largest upside, not in consensus).

  • Scenario (Morgan Stanley): the European net cost target doubles to about EUR 2bn and extends to the EUR 10bn emerging-market cost base, adding 7 percent to FY30 EBITDAaL and 26 percent to free cash flow.
  • Effect on EPS: if EUR 0.5bn of net, wholly owned European EBITDAaL reaches the accounts by FY29 and EUR 1.0bn by FY31, FY29 EPS rises 1.7 cents (+14 percent) and FY31 EPS 4.0 cents (+25 percent). A cost to achieve of about EUR 1bn over two to three years reduces buyback capacity by a similar amount (-3 percent of EPS), so the net effect is about +11 percent in FY29 and +22 percent by FY31.
  • Timing: board representation follows UK clearance, in summer 2027 at the earliest; a target could be announced in H2 FY28 and reach the accounts from FY29.
  • Precedent: Tele2's gains lasted two to three years, then faded; Altice's cuts damaged customer retention. Vodafone Germany, last on network quality, is where an aggressive cut would most likely cost revenue.
  • Watch: the UK national-security decision; Vega's stake settling out of the bank block trades; any change to the incentive plan.

And the multiple, which outweighs all five judgements. Each 1.0x on about EUR 0.13 of two-year-forward EPS is worth EUR 0.13 a share, about 11p or 9.5 percent of the price. From today's 10.7x, a move to 12x is worth +12 percent, to 13.4x +25 percent and to 16x +50 percent, while a fall to 8.3x costs 22 percent. The five judgements together span roughly -25 percent to +25 percent on FY29 EPS; the multiple alone spans -22 percent to +50 percent on the price.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Bottom lineVodafone is a better and more predictable company than it was three years ago, but its investment case is weaker than its business case, because three narrowings sit between EBITDAaL and the shareholder. The market has over-credited the per-share story, and the next six months are more likely to correct that than the following twelve.

The business case is strong and predictable. The portfolio is fixed, the UK is wholly owned and integrating ahead of plan, Africa is consolidated and growing, the cost programme is funded, and the incentive plan pays management for cash. The operating forecasts for the next 18 months are arithmetic on announced facts, and the company guides them with an honest tracker's record.

The investment case is weaker, because three narrowings sit between EBITDAaL and the shareholder.

  1. Vodafone owns all of its shrinking German profit and only about a third of its growing Kenyan profit.
  2. The FY26 earnings base borrowed EUR 1.4bn of investment income on disposal cash that is now spent.
  3. From FY28, per-share growth comes from a buyback that is half funded by debt and that reverses if EBITDAaL stalls.

The market has priced the operating story correctly and the per-share story generously. Consensus FY28 EPS sits at our bull case, and the shares trade at a company-specific premium while the sector trades at trough multiples.

The skew turns with time. The events of the next six months have a negative skew to expectations; the events of months six to eighteen have a positive skew; and the events of months eighteen to thirty-six are known to the sell-side but under-weighted by investors.

The value. The fair multiple is about 12x two-year-forward earnings, not the guideline's 16x. At 12x, the probable 18-month return is in the mid-teens with a wide cone, driven by buybacks and the dividend.

The decision. The unusually positive skew Richard looks for is not present at today's price. It would be present at about 100p, with FY28 consensus reset and the May 2027 catalysts still ahead, and the next two results events are the likeliest route to that state.

B

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength

A completed reset, a closed and wholly owned merger with dated synergies, a funded cost programme and an activist owner with a cost-cutting record, held back only by the absence of any force acting on the German consumer franchise.

C

Foundations' Robustness

Below-average returns (5.5 percent post-tax ROCE), margins and earnings quality, a cable asset being overbuilt in the largest profit pool, and a third of profit minority-shared and earned in emerging-market currencies, offset by a comfortable, long-dated balance sheet, low cash tax and predictable guided lines.

C

Setups' Fit/Crispness

The case takes the form of a Big Corporate Change-driven EPS Upgrader (EPSU): a portfolio reset, a merger and owner-forced cost cuts. But the step-up is diluted before it reaches earnings per share: FY27 EPS is flat, FY28 EPS is +6 percent, and the double-digit growth after that comes from the buyback. The case therefore does not match that setup cleanly. Nor does it match the Mechanical EPS Upgrader setup, because Vodafone is not a serial acquirer and upgrades are not in prospect for 12 months.

C

Case Riskiness

Simple and trackable at the operating level, noisy and half-blind at the per-share level, with a concentrated list of external risks (currency, a German competitor, a Kenyan court, the bond market) and a 1.5 beta to a de-rating sector.

End notes

  • Conventions. Fiscal years end 31 March (FY27 is the year to March 2027). Money is in euros unless stated. Profit is adjusted EBITDAaL (EBITDA after leases), the basis of company guidance and of FactSet's brokers'-basis consensus (FY26: EUR 11,351m, a 28.1 percent margin). Earnings per share is the company's adjusted figure on the brokers' basis (FY26: 10.72 eurocents). "Our forecasts" are the Financial Analyst's model of record (model update 2), the forecasts this memo uses. Consensus is the FactSet median of 27 October 2026.
  • Two notes on the model's basis. The model summary's "+68.7 percent" FY27 EPS growth is a basis artefact: it measures against the Viewforth-definition FY26 EPS of EUR 0.063, not the brokers' EUR 0.107, and on the brokers' basis FY27 EPS is flat. The model's EPS is after minorities, because the composite net-financial-items input carries minorities grossed up at the tax rate; the summary's template line saying otherwise should be ignored.
  • Total shareholder return split. The split of the model's return into dividends, the multiple and earnings in #12 is the template's own.
  • Acronyms. CMA: Competition and Markets Authority (UK). ECJ: European Court of Justice. MBNL: Mobile Broadband Network Limited, the UK network-sharing joint venture. BNetzA: Bundesnetzagentur, the German network regulator. OXG: Vodafone's German fibre joint venture. DOCSIS: the cable broadband standard. ROCE: return on capital employed.
  • Default visuals are from the Master Dashboard and the default visual set built from model update 2; each figure's note gives its basis. FactSet history in the long financials table is the reported basis (adjusted EBITDA, reported earnings per share), which differs from the brokers' EBITDAaL basis used in the memo.
  • Charts in visuals/drawn were drawn for this page from the memo's own figures. In the EBITDAaL bridge, "other and rounding" (EUR 0.24bn) reconciles the stated segment steps to the stated totals; in the net income bridge, "tax and other" is the residual after the stated, approximate depreciation, financing and minority steps.
  • Three further charts (segment EBITDAaL in #6, twelve-month share price changes in #8, and buyback funding in Judgement 3) were drawn for this edition from the memo's own figures. In the segment chart, segments do not sum to the group total, and Other Europe's stated EUR 1.75bn to 1.95bn is read as FY27 to FY31.
  • In the judgements chart, each bar is the downside and upside named in that judgement; the below-the-line bar refers to FY28 EPS, the others to FY29, and the multiple to the share price.
  • Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Holdings in associates: 6,492.0, 19.5% of market capitalisation.
